# Tutorial Summary: Complex Exponentials and Phasors in Spatial Fourier Transforms

# Core Concepts

## Phasors vs. Complex Exponentials:
A phasor is a static complex representation defining two fixed parameters: amplitude and phase (A e^{j\phi}).
The complex exponential provides the varying wave carrier (spatial or temporal) that multiplies the phasor.
In time-domain signals, multiplying a phasor by e^{j\omega t} rotates the vector around the complex origin as time advances.

## Transition to the Spatial Domain:
In 2D spatial contexts (replacing time t with coordinates (x, y)), the complex exponential takes the form e^{j(k_x x + k_y y)}.
The phase varies continuously across physical coordinates rather than advancing over time, generating a spatial wave pattern.

## Fourier Plane Representation:
A single spatial harmonic does not trace out a continuous circle in the frequency domain.
Instead, it maps to discrete points located at its specific spatial frequency coordinates.
Conjugate Symmetry and the "Complex Exponential Tax":

## Real-world spatial signals are purely real-valued.
Using complex exponentials requires expressing a real harmonic (such as a cosine wave) via Euler's formula: \cos(k x) = \frac{e^{j k x} + e^{-j k x}}{2}
This creates conjugate symmetry, resulting in two distinct points in the Fourier plane (positive and negative frequency components).
During the inverse transform, the imaginary components of the conjugate pair cancel out entirely, reconstructing the original real signalâ€”a trade-off humorously framed as the "complex exponential tax" for enjoying linear algebraic and notation convenience.
